claim: The function of a neural circuit is shaped by the computations performed by its interneurons, which in many cases are not easily accessible to experimental investigation.
source: The function of a neural circuit is shaped by the computations performed by its interneurons, which in many cases are not easily accessible to experimental investigation.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural circuits based on established scientific understanding.

claim: OFF midget ganglion cells subserve high-resolution vision.
source: The results reveal nonlinear subunits in the circuity of OFF midget ganglion cells, which subserve high-resolution vision.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of OFF midget ganglion cells in the visual system.

claim: The subunit model explains light responses to a variety of stimuli more accurately than a linear model.
source: The model explains light responses to a variety of stimuli more accurately than a linear model, including stimuli targeted to cones within and across subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing model predictions to actual responses.

claim: The recovered model components are consistent with known anatomical organization of midget bipolar interneurons.
source: The recovered model components are consistent with known anatomical organization of midget bipolar interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model results with anatomical data and established knowledge.

claim: Cones, bipolar cells, and retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) form a two-tier cascade of linear and nonlinear processing in the retina.
source: In the retina, cones, bipolar cells, and retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) form a two-tier cascade of linear and nonlinear processing that is thought to underlie many important visual functions (see Schwartz and Rieke, 2011; Gollisch, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nonlinear subunit computation has been observed in the responses of several types of RGCs.
source: A notable example is the nonlinear subunit computation (Hochstein and Shapley, 1976) observed in the responses of several types of RGCs, the output neurons of the retina.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Cone signals are first combined by bipolar interneurons, whose outputs are rectified at the synapse onto RGCs.
source: Instead, cone signals are first combined by bipolar interneurons, whose outputs are rectified at the synapse onto RGCs (Demb et al., 1999, 2001; Borghuis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nonlinear architecture endows the RGC receptive field with localized subunits that permit the representation of finer spatial detail than would be expected given the overall receptive field size.
source: This nonlinear architecture endows the RGC receptive field with localized subunits that permit the representation of finer spatial detail than would be expected given the overall receptive field size (Hochstein and Shapley, 1976; Lee et al., 1995; Demb et al., 2001; Baccus et al., 2008; Crook et al., 2008; Schwartz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Subunits have been implicated in the processing of features like object motion and looming.
source: Subunits have also been implicated in the processing of features like object motion and looming (Olveczky et al., 2007; Münch et al., 2009), and some of their functional characteristics have been inferred for various cell types and species (Enroth-Cugell and Robson, 1966; Hochstein and Shapley, 1976; Victor and Shapley, 1979a, 1979b; Enroth-Cugell and Freeman, 1987; Bölinger and Gollisch, 2012; Schwartz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The spatial organization of convergent cone input onto nonlinear subunits has never been visualized, nor mapped across a population of RGCs.
source: However, the spatial organization of convergent cone input onto nonlinear subunits has never been visualized, nor mapped across a population of RGCs.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current work relative to previous literature.

claim: Independent stimulation of individual cones and pairs of cones revealed significant nonlinear interactions within the receptive fields of OFF midget RGCs.
source: Independent stimulation of individual cones and pairs of cones revealed significant nonlinear interactions within the receptive fields of OFF midget RGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cone pair stimulation experiments.

claim: A cascade model and an associated fitting method were developed to capture nonlinear response properties of OFF midget RGCs.
source: A cascade model and an associated fitting method were developed to capture these nonlinear response properties.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach developed in the study.

claim: The model revealed the spatial structure of nonlinear interactions in the individual cone inputs to each OFF midget RGC.
source: The model revealed the spatial structure of nonlinear interactions in the individual cone inputs to each OFF midget RGC, and enabled adaptive generation of validation stimuli targeted to specific cones during experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of model fitting to experimental data.

claim: When fitted to entire populations of OFF midget RGCs, the model revealed a spatial organization of nonlinear subunits consistent with the known anatomical convergence of cones to midget bipolar cells.
source: When fitted to entire populations of OFF midget RGCs, the model revealed a spatial organization of nonlinear subunits consistent with the known anatomical convergence of cones to midget bipolar cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model results with anatomical data.

claim: OFF midget cells exhibited the largest signal-to-noise ratios and response stability over recordings.
source: Experiments and analyses focused on the responses of OFF midget cells over a range of eccentricities. These cells exhibited the largest signal-to-noise ratios and response stability over recordings.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data justifying the focus on OFF midget cells.

claim: Many OFF midget cells responded robustly to decrements of light presented to either of a pair of cones individually, but also responded robustly when a decrement of light was presented to one cone and an increment of the same contrast was presented simultaneously to the other cone.
source: Many cells exhibited non-linear responses to opposite polarity stimulation of cone pairs (Figure 1A,B). Specifically, many OFF midget cells responded robustly to decrements of light presented to either of a pair of cones individually, but also responded robustly when a decrement of light was presented to one cone and an increment of the same contrast was presented simultaneously to the other cone (for 73/78 cone pairs tested from 13 RGCs, response to paired stimulations was at least 50% of the response to single cone decrements alone).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired cone stimulation experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: For 73/78 cone pairs tested from 13 RGCs, response to paired stimulations was at least 50% of the response to single cone decrements alone.
source: for 73/78 cone pairs tested from 13 RGCs, response to paired stimulations was at least 50% of the response to single cone decrements alone
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the paired cone stimulation experiments.

claim: Only a small number (5/78) of cone pairs yielded response cancellation.
source: Only a small number (5/78) of cone pairs yielded response cancellation (see example in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the paired cone stimulation experiments.

claim: Failures of cancellation indicate significant spatial nonlinearities within OFF midget cell receptive fields.
source: These failures of cancellation indicate significant spatial nonlinearities within OFF midget cell receptive fields.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations of failure of cancellation.

claim: OFF midget bipolar cells linearly combine convergent cone input, but introduce a rectifying nonlinearity at the synapse with RGCs.
source: These examples are consistent with the following interpretation suggested by preceding work in other species and cell types: OFF midget bipolar cells (which carry cone signals to OFF midget RGCs) (Kolb and Marshak, 2003) linearly combine convergent cone input, but introduce a rectifying nonlinearity at the synapse with RGCs (Demb et al., 2001; Bölinger and Gollisch, 2012; Schwartz et al., 2012).
evidence: This interpretation is based on citations to previous work and inference from the current data.

claim: The cancellation of opposing signals from a pair of cones indicates that the cones converge on a single midget bipolar cell.
source: In this interpretation, the cancellation of opposing signals from a pair of cones indicates that the cones converge on a single midget bipolar cell, while failure of cancellation indicates that the cones provide input to distinct midget bipolar cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on the proposed model.

claim: Failure of cancellation indicates that the cones provide input to distinct midget bipolar cells.
source: In this interpretation, the cancellation of opposing signals from a pair of cones indicates that the cones converge on a single midget bipolar cell, while failure of cancellation indicates that the cones provide input to distinct midget bipolar cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on the proposed model.

claim: The paired stimulation approach is not suitable for characterizing large populations of cones and RGCs, because it relies on testing a small number of cone pairs, in a small number of RGCs per retina.
source: The paired stimulation approach described above is not suitable for characterizing large populations of cones and RGCs, because it relies on testing a small number of cone pairs, in a small number of RGCs per retina.
evidence: This is a logical assessment of the limitations of the paired stimulation method.

claim: Testing all cone pairs in all RGCs is infeasible.
source: Testing all cone pairs in all RGCs is infeasible.
evidence: This is a practical assessment of experimental feasibility.

claim: It is possible to identify the presence of an intermediate nonlinearity and the specific pairs (or groups) of cone signals that combine linearly in a common subunit by fitting a single hierarchical model to the responses of RGCs under random stimulation with spatiotemporal noise.
source: It is possible, however, to identify the two key properties of interest—the presence of an intermediate nonlinearity, and the specific pairs (or groups) of cone signals that combine linearly in a common subunit—by fitting a single hierarchical model to the responses of RGCs under random stimulation with spatiotemporal noise.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: The hierarchical model has two stages of linear integration and an intervening static nonlinearity.
source: We developed a hierarchical model with two stages of linear integration and an intervening static nonlinearity (Figure 2) mirroring the known elements of the underlying circuitry (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the structure of the model developed in the study.

claim: Subsets of one or more cones are assigned to 'subunits', which are assumed to be non-overlapping to ensure unique solutions during fitting.
source: First, subsets of one or more cones are assigned to 'subunits', which are assumed to be non-overlapping to ensure unique solutions during fitting, that is, a cone cannot provide input to multiple subunits (see 'Materials and methods'); this assumption is biologically sensible given evidence for minimal overlap in bipolar dendritic trees (Wässle et al., 1994) and little divergence from cones to OFF midget bipolar cells (Kolb and Marshak, 2003).
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the model, justified by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: There is minimal overlap in bipolar dendritic trees.
source: this assumption is biologically sensible given evidence for minimal overlap in bipolar dendritic trees (Wässle et al., 1994) and little divergence from cones to OFF midget bipolar cells (Kolb and Marshak, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to anatomical studies.

claim: There is little divergence from cones to OFF midget bipolar cells.
source: this assumption is biologically sensible given evidence for minimal overlap in bipolar dendritic trees (Wässle et al., 1994) and little divergence from cones to OFF midget bipolar cells (Kolb and Marshak, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to anatomical studies.

claim: The model was fitted to hundreds of simultaneously recorded OFF midget RGCs by measuring responses to high-resolution spatio-temporal noise.
source: The model was fitted to hundreds of simultaneously recorded OFF midget RGCs by measuring responses to high-resolution spatio-temporal noise (Field et al., 2010) (15 retinas total, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used to fit the model.

claim: For most cells, the estimated subunit nonlinearity approximated half-wave rectification.
source: For most cells, the estimated subunit nonlinearity approximated half-wave rectification, consistent with the failures of cancellation observed in paired stimulation.
evidence: This is a result from fitting the model to experimental data.

claim: Many OFF midget RGCs had only single-cone subunits (48 ± 10%, percentage ±s.e.m. across retinas).
source: Many OFF midget RGCs had only single-cone subunits (48 ± 10%, percentage ±s.e.m. across retinas).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from model fitting across multiple retinas.

claim: The remaining cells generally had subunits with two (27 ± 6% OFF midgets) or three (13 ± 4% OFF midgets) cones.
source: The remaining cells generally had subunits with two (27 ± 6% OFF midgets) or three (13 ± 4% OFF midgets) cones.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from model fitting across multiple retinas.

claim: The subunit model showed an improvement of 18 ± 3% (mean ± s.e.m.) over the LN model across 15 retinas.
source: We found an improvement of 18 ± 3% (mean ± s.e.m.) across 15 retinas (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing model performance across retinas.

claim: Model accuracies on 'maximally differentiating' test stimuli revealed a larger improvement of 92 ± 26%.
source: Model accuracies on these 'maximally differentiating' test stimuli revealed a larger improvement of 92 ± 26% (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from model comparison on selected stimuli.

claim: Variation in improvement across retinas may have arisen from differences in physiological state across tissue preparations.
source: Variation in improvement across retinas (Figure 3D) may have arisen from differences in physiological state across tissue preparations (see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is speculation about the source of variability in the results.

claim: Accuracy for the subunit model was 51 ± 1% R2 adj. (mean ± s.e.m. across 68 OFF midget RGCs from one retina).
source: Accuracy for the subunit model was 51 ± 1% R2 adj. (mean ± s.e.m. across 68 OFF midget RGCs from one retina), and improvement over the LN model was 40% (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from model evaluation on repeated noise stimuli.

claim: Improvement of the subunit model over the LN model was 40% on repeated noise stimuli.
source: Accuracy for the subunit model was 51 ± 1% R2 adj. (mean ± s.e.m. across 68 OFF midget RGCs from one retina), and improvement over the LN model was 40% (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from model comparison on repeated noise stimuli.

claim: At low spatial frequencies, OFF midget RGC responses were modulated at the temporal frequency of the stimulus.
source: At low spatial frequencies (period matched approximately to the size of the receptive field), responses were modulated at the temporal frequency of the stimulus.
evidence: This is an observation from grating stimulation experiments.

claim: At higher spatial frequencies, OFF midget RGC responses were modulated at twice the temporal frequency of the stimulus, for at least some spatial phases.
source: But at higher spatial frequencies, their responses were modulated at twice the temporal frequency of the stimulus, for at least some spatial phases.
evidence: This is an observation from grating stimulation experiments showing frequency doubling.

claim: The rectifying nonlinearities within the fitted subunit model were sufficient to predict frequency doubling.
source: The rectifying nonlinearities within the fitted subunit model were sufficient to predict this frequency doubling, whereas the LN model exhibited dominant response modulation at the frequency of the stimulus (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result showing that the subunit model can predict the observed frequency doubling behavior.

claim: Accuracy of the subunit model on grating stimuli was 83 ± 1% R2 adj. (mean ± s.e.m. across 32 RGCs).
source: Across the population, accuracy of the subunit model was 83 ± 1% R2 adj. (mean ± s.e.m. across 32 RGCs), and improvement in predictive performance of the subunit model over the LN model was 28 ± 2% (mean ± bootstrapped confidence interval) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from model evaluation on grating stimuli.

claim: Improvement in predictive performance of the subunit model over the LN model on grating stimuli was 28 ± 2% (mean ± bootstrapped confidence interval).
source: Across the population, accuracy of the subunit model was 83 ± 1% R2 adj. (mean ± s.e.m. across 32 RGCs), and improvement in predictive performance of the subunit model over the LN model was 28 ± 2% (mean ± bootstrapped confidence interval) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from model comparison on grating stimuli.

claim: Improvement was more pronounced at higher spatial frequencies, ranging from 10 ± 1% (at a frequency where one cycle spanned the entire RF) to 50 ± 6% (at a frequency where each cycle spanned 1–2 cones).
source: Improvement was more pronounced at higher spatial frequencies (Figure 5C), ranging from 10 ± 1% (at a frequency where one cycle spanned the entire RF) to 50 ± 6% (at a frequency where each cycle spanned 1–2 cones), and was significant at all frequencies (paired t-test, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a quantitative result showing spatial frequency dependence of model improvement.

claim: The improvement of the subunit model over the LN model was significant at all spatial frequencies (paired t-test, p < 0.0001).
source: Improvement was more pronounced at higher spatial frequencies (Figure 5C), ranging from 10 ± 1% (at a frequency where one cycle spanned the entire RF) to 50 ± 6% (at a frequency where each cycle spanned 1–2 cones), and was significant at all frequencies (paired t-test, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing model performance across spatial frequencies.

claim: The improvement of the full fitted subunit model over a simpler model with all subunits as single cones was small: roughly 0–10% across all RGCs.
source: Although the subunit model provided large improvements over an LN model, the improvement of the full fitted subunit model over a simpler model with all subunits as single cones was small: roughly 0–10% across all RGCs (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing different versions of the subunit model.

claim: The small difference in model performance was likely due to the small size and number of multi-cone subunits per RGC—typically no more than a few subunits with two or three cones—and the simplistic spatial structure of the stimuli used.
source: The small difference was likely due to the small size and number of multi-cone subunits per RGC—typically no more than a few subunits with two or three cones—and the simplistic spatial structure of the stimuli used.
evidence: This is an interpretation of why the improvement was small.

claim: For RGCs at small eccentricities, the fraction of subunits recovered by the model including 1–2 cones was consistent with the fraction expected based on anatomical observations made separately.
source: For RGCs at small eccentricities, the fraction of subunits recovered by the model including 1–2 cones was consistent with the fraction expected based on anatomical observations made separately (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a comparison between model results and anatomical data.

claim: For larger eccentricities, the model recovered larger subunits, also generally in agreement with anatomical observations.
source: For larger eccentricities, the model recovered larger subunits, also generally in agreement with anatomical observations.
evidence: This is a comparison between model results and anatomical data.

claim: For cones within subunits, RGC responses to inputs of opposite polarity were at least partially cancelled, whereas responses to cones in separate subunits exhibited little cancellation.
source: Responses to combined increment and decrement stimulation were qualitatively consistent with the predictions of the model: For cones within subunits, RGC responses to inputs of opposite polarity were at least partially cancelled, whereas responses to cones in separate subunits exhibited little cancellation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a result from closed-loop validation experiments.

claim: Across 252 cone pairs tested (from 21 RGCs), the responses were significantly more accurately predicted by the full subunit model (r2 = 0.24) than by either a model with single-cone subunits (r2 = 0.11) or an LN model (r2 = 0.10) (both p < 0.005, bootstrap test).
source: Quantitatively, across 252 cone pairs tested (from 21 RGCs), the responses were significantly more accurately predicted by the full subunit model (r2 = 0.24) than by either a model with single-cone subunits (r2 = 0.11) or an LN model (r2 = 0.10) (both p < 0.005, bootstrap test, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a quantitative result from closed-loop validation experiments with statistical testing.

claim: In the cat retina, 'X' cells were defined as those that sum visual input linearly within the spatial receptive field, whereas 'Y' cells were defined as those that exhibited nonlinear behaviors (notably, frequency-doubling).
source: In the cat retina, 'X' cells were defined as those that sum visual input linearly within the spatial receptive field, whereas 'Y' cells were defined as those that exhibited nonlinear behaviors (notably, frequency-doubling) (Enroth-Cugell and Robson, 1966; Hochstein and Shapley, 1976).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous literature on cat retinal ganglion cells.

claim: X and Y cells have been associated with the morphologically distinct beta and alpha RGCs.
source: These functionally defined classes have been associated with the morphologically distinct beta and alpha RGCs (Boycott and Wässle, 1974; Peichl and Wässle, 1981; Wässle et al., 1981a, 1981b).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous literature.

claim: The magnocellular-projecting parasol RGCs have been shown to exhibit nonlinearities similar to Y cells.
source: The magnocellular-projecting parasol RGCs have been shown to exhibit nonlinearities similar to Y cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies of primate retinal ganglion cells.

claim: The parvocellular-projecting midget RGCs have usually been likened to linear X cells.
source: In contrast, the parvocellular-projecting midget RGCs have usually been likened to linear X cells (Shapley et al., 1981; Kaplan and Shapley, 1982; Derrington and Lennie, 1984; Levitt et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a summary of previous literature on midget RGCs.

claim: The nonlinearities revealed in this study are inconsistent with the interpretation that midget RGCs are linear X cells.
source: The nonlinearities revealed here (Figures 1, 4, 6) are inconsistent with this interpretation, as are previous in vivo studies of parvocellular-projecting cells (Derrington and Lennie, 1984) and ex vivo studies of midget RGCs (Petrusca et al., 2007; Cafaro and Rieke, 2013), which demonstrated modest but clear frequency-doubling in response to contrast reversing visual stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current results in the context of previous literature.

claim: Previous in vivo studies of parvocellular-projecting cells and ex vivo studies of midget RGCs demonstrated modest but clear frequency-doubling in response to contrast reversing visual stimuli.
source: The nonlinearities revealed here (Figures 1, 4, 6) are inconsistent with this interpretation, as are previous in vivo studies of parvocellular-projecting cells (Derrington and Lennie, 1984) and ex vivo studies of midget RGCs (Petrusca et al., 2007; Cafaro and Rieke, 2013), which demonstrated modest but clear frequency-doubling in response to contrast reversing visual stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies.

claim: Many previous in vivo studies probed midget cell responses in the central retina, where the receptive field center consists of a single cone, and thus, a single subunit.
source: First, many previous in vivo studies probed midget cell responses in the central retina, where the receptive field center consists of a single cone, and thus, a single subunit.
evidence: This is an explanation for discrepancies with previous literature based on methodological differences.

claim: In cases where the entire receptive field is formed by the cone collecting aperture, it would be expected to exhibit the linear summation of incident light intensity performed by the cone.
source: In such cases, the entire receptive field is formed by the cone collecting aperture, and would be expected to exhibit the linear summation of incident light intensity performed by the cone.
evidence: This is a logical inference about expected behavior in single-cone receptive fields.

claim: In vivo studies were typically performed using anesthetics that could raise the basal release of neurotransmitter from bipolar cells.
source: Second, in vivo studies were typically performed using anesthetics that could raise the basal release of neurotransmitter from bipolar cells, and low basal release rates are thought to underlie at least part of the rectifying subunit nonlinearity (Robbins and Ikeda, 1989; Demb et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an explanation for discrepancies with previous literature based on methodological differences, supported by citations.

claim: Low basal release rates are thought to underlie at least part of the rectifying subunit nonlinearity.
source: Second, in vivo studies were typically performed using anesthetics that could raise the basal release of neurotransmitter from bipolar cells, and low basal release rates are thought to underlie at least part of the rectifying subunit nonlinearity (Robbins and Ikeda, 1989; Demb et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Variability in basal release rates could account for some of the variability across preparations observed in this study.
source: Indeed, variability in basal release rates could account for some of the variability across preparations observed here (Figures 3D, 6).
evidence: This is speculation about the source of variability in the results.

claim: Although OFF midget RGCs exhibit nonlinear spatial summation not found in X cells, they are also different from Y cells.
source: Although OFF midget RGCs exhibit nonlinear spatial summation not found in X cells, they are also different from Y cells.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the properties of different cell types.

claim: The most commonly stated defining characteristic for Y cells is a frequency doubled response to a contrast reversing grating, with a magnitude that is independent of the spatial phase of the stimulus.
source: The most commonly stated defining characteristic for Y cells is a frequency doubled response to a contrast reversing grating, with a magnitude that is independent of the spatial phase of the stimulus (Enroth-Cugell and Robson, 1966; Hochstein and Shapley, 1976; Crook et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Y cells from previous literature.

claim: Although midget cells exhibited frequency doubling in response to contrast reversing gratings, the magnitude was phase dependent.
source: Although midget cells exhibited frequency doubling in response to contrast reversing gratings (Figure 5), the magnitude was phase dependent (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the grating experiments.

claim: Phase dependence may arise both from the low occurrence of multi-cone subunits, and the fact that midget cells receive input from only one bipolar cell type, which forms a single mosaic with minimal dendritic overlap.
source: Phase dependence may arise both from the low occurrence of multi-cone subunits, and the fact that midget cells receive input from only one bipolar cell type, which forms a single mosaic with minimal dendritic overlap (Wässle et al., 1994).
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed phase dependence, supported by citation to anatomical data.

claim: The ON and OFF parasol RGC populations exhibit properties consistent with the Y cell definition.
source: In contrast, the ON and OFF parasol RGC populations, which exhibit properties consistent with the Y cell definition (Petrusca et al., 2007; Crook et al., 2008), receive input primarily from two bipolar cell types (Bordt et al., 2006; Calkins and Sterling, 2007), each of which receive convergent input from many cones, and overlap each other in space, and thus would be expected to exhibit greater phase invariance.
evidence: This is a comparison with parasol cells supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Parasol RGCs receive input primarily from two bipolar cell types, each of which receive convergent input from many cones, and overlap each other in space.
source: In contrast, the ON and OFF parasol RGC populations, which exhibit properties consistent with the Y cell definition (Petrusca et al., 2007; Crook et al., 2008), receive input primarily from two bipolar cell types (Bordt et al., 2006; Calkins and Sterling, 2007), each of which receive convergent input from many cones, and overlap each other in space, and thus would be expected to exhibit greater phase invariance.
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge about parasol cells from previous studies.

claim: Lack of phase independence in midget cells may also arise from differences between feed-forward and crossover inhibition that shapes midget vs parasol RGC responses respectively.
source: Lack of phase independence in midget cells may also arise from differences between feed-forward and crossover inhibition that shapes midget vs parasol RGC responses respectively (Cafaro and Rieke, 2013).
evidence: This is an alternative explanation supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The firing rates obtained in the present work are somewhat lower than those found in anesthetized in vivo recordings.
source: The firing rates obtained in the present work are somewhat lower than those found in anesthetized in vivo recordings (Troy and Lee, 1994).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current results with previous in vivo studies.

claim: Nonlinear spatial summation was observed in midget cells exhibiting a range of spontaneous firing rates from 0 to 10 spikes/s.
source: Nonlinear spatial summation (as in Figure 1A,B) was observed in midget cells exhibiting a range of spontaneous firing rates from 0 to 10 spikes/s (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: It remains uncertain whether and to what degree ex vivo recordings, or in vivo recordings under anesthesia, reflect a more natural state with respect to the signals studied.
source: It remains uncertain whether and to what degree these ex vivo recordings, or in vivo recordings under anesthesia, reflect a more natural state with respect to the signals studied.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty about the physiological relevance of the preparation.

claim: The confirmation of the biological relevance of nonlinear signaling by OFF midget cells awaits a decisive test in awake behaving animals.
source: The confirmation of the biological relevance of nonlinear signaling by OFF midget cells awaits a decisive test in awake behaving animals.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed to confirm the findings.

claim: The model developed here was inspired by previous subunit models, general successes in maximum likelihood fitting of neural models to spiking responses, and recent efforts to fit subunit-like models to V1 complex cells.
source: The model developed here was inspired by previous subunit models (Victor and Shapley, 1979b), general successes in maximum likelihood fitting of neural models to spiking responses (Paninski, 2004; Truccolo et al., 2005; Ahrens et al., 2008; Pillow et al., 2008), and recent efforts to fit subunit-like models to V1 complex cells (Rust et al., 2005; Vintch et al., 2012; Lochmann et al., 2013; McFarland et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the intellectual context and inspiration for the modeling approach.

claim: The model expresses subunit computations directly in terms of elementary circuit components: photoreceptors, inferred bipolar cells, and ganglion cells.
source: First, the model expresses subunit computations directly in terms of elementary circuit components: photoreceptors, inferred bipolar cells, and ganglion cells.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the model that distinguishes it from previous approaches.

claim: Unlike some previous efforts to characterize subunits, all components of the model used here were fitted based on a single ensemble of stimuli and spiking responses, rather than inferred separately based on responses to specialized stimuli.
source: Second, unlike some previous efforts to characterize subunits (Victor and Shapley, 1979b), all components of the model used here were fitted based on a single ensemble of stimuli and spiking responses, rather than inferred separately based on responses to specialized stimuli.
evidence: This describes a methodological advantage of the current approach over previous methods.

claim: Simultaneous fitting is a generally preferable strategy for optimization, because it allows the parameters to work together to explain observed responses.
source: Simultaneous fitting is a generally preferable strategy for optimization, because it allows the parameters to work together to explain observed responses.
evidence: This is a general principle of optimization and model fitting.

claim: Unlike some approaches (e.g., spike-triggered covariance or maximally-informative dimensions), which have recovered stimulus features that are unique only up to an arbitrary linear transformation, this method recovers a unique solution for the spatial structure of subunits.
source: Finally, unlike some approaches (e.g., spike-triggered covariance [Strong et al., 1998; Brenner et al., 2000; Rust et al., 2005; Touryan et al., 2005; Pillow and Simoncelli, 2006; Schwartz et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2007] or maximally-informative dimensions [Sharpee et al., 2004]), which have recovered stimulus features that are unique only up to an arbitrary linear transformation, this method recovers a unique solution for the spatial structure of subunits.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the current method over previous approaches, supported by citations.

claim: One study used a closed-loop experiment to find combinations of stimuli eliciting constant RGC responses, and used the shapes of the resulting iso-response contours in stimulus space to dissociate linear and nonlinear integration.
source: One study (Bölinger and Gollisch, 2012) used a closed-loop experiment to find combinations of stimuli eliciting constant RGC responses, and used the shapes of the resulting iso-response contours in stimulus space to dissociate linear and nonlinear integration.
evidence: This is a description of a complementary approach from previous literature.

claim: Iso-response contour mapping has only proven practically useful with stimuli defined in two or three dimensions.
source: While elegant, iso-response contour mapping has only proven practically useful with stimuli defined in two or three dimensions (Bölinger and Gollisch, 2012; Horwitz and Hass, 2012), whereas the current model operated on the full set of cone inputs to each RGC (typically 5–15 dimensions).
evidence: This is a comparison highlighting a limitation of the iso-response contour method relative to the current approach.

claim: Another study developed a model for responses of ON alpha-like mouse RGCs by combining detailed morphological measurements with direct physiological measurements from bipolars and RGCs.
source: Another study (Schwartz et al., 2012) developed a model for responses of ON alpha-like mouse RGCs by combining detailed morphological measurements with direct physiological measurements from bipolars and RGCs.
evidence: This is a description of another complementary approach from previous literature.

claim: The functional approach taken here, while lacking the firm anatomical foundation, can extend more readily to describing computations in complete neuronal populations and in multiple cell types.
source: The functional approach taken here, while lacking the firm anatomical foundation, can extend more readily to describing computations in complete neuronal populations (Figure 6) and in multiple cell types.
evidence: This is a comparison highlighting advantages of the current approach.

claim: The model developed here does not account for electrical coupling between photoreceptors which could produce cancellation of increment and decrement stimuli delivered to neighboring cones.
source: The model developed here does not account for electrical coupling between photoreceptors (Tsukamoto et al., 1992; Hornstein et al., 2004; O'Brien et al., 2012) which could produce cancellation of increment and decrement stimuli delivered to neighboring cones.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the model, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: A study of cone electrical coupling in primate retina suggested that signal mixing is modest.
source: A study of cone electrical coupling in primate retina suggested that signal mixing is modest (Hornstein et al., 2004), thus it is probably unable to account for the cancellation observed.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a previous study.

claim: Since many cone pairs tested exhibited little or no cancellation, any effects of adjacent cone coupling are likely to be weak or sporadic.
source: However, since many cone pairs tested exhibited little or no cancellation (e.g., Figure 1), any effects of adjacent cone coupling are likely to be weak or sporadic.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Connexin-36 immunolabeling revealed ubiquitous expression at junctions between nearly all neighboring cones, in both central and peripheral primate retina.
source: In contrast to this prediction, connexin-36 immunolabeling revealed ubiquitous expression at junctions between nearly all neighboring cones, in both central and peripheral primate retina (O'Brien et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of anatomical findings from a previous study.

claim: The observed eccentricity dependence of the spatial extent of cancellation implies that for the present results to be explained by cone coupling, the coupling would have to increase substantially with eccentricity.
source: Also, the observed eccentricity dependence of the spatial extent of cancellation (Figure 6) implies that for the present results to be explained by cone coupling, the coupling would have to increase substantially with eccentricity.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The model described here could potentially capture nonlinear computations in other RGC types, such as ON midget or parasol RGCs.
source: The model described here could potentially capture nonlinear computations in other RGC types, such as ON midget or parasol RGCs.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the model.

claim: Unlike midget RGCs, parasol RGCs receive input from more than one type of bipolar cell, and the receptive fields of these bipolar cells likely exhibit substantial spatial overlap.
source: For example, unlike midget RGCs, parasol RGCs receive input from more than one type of bipolar cell, and the receptive fields of these bipolar cells likely exhibit substantial spatial overlap, whereas the current model assumes nonoverlapping subunits (Figure 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge about parasol cell anatomy.

claim: Preliminary model fits of parasol responses produce subunits smaller than what is expected from anatomical data, as would be expected in the case of two overlapping bipolar populations.
source: Indeed, preliminary model fits of parasol responses produce subunits smaller than what is expected from anatomical data, as would be expected in the case of two overlapping bipolar populations (Boycott and Wässle, 1991) (not shown).
evidence: This is a preliminary observation from applying the model to parasol cells.

claim: Subunit overlap may underlie the reported Y-cell invariance to spatial phase.
source: Subunit overlap may underlie the reported Y-cell invariance to spatial phase (see above), and is thus an important goal for future modeling.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying Y-cell properties.

claim: The current model does not include receptive field surrounds.
source: For example, the current model does not include receptive field surrounds.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the current model.

claim: Insofar as surrounds reflect the contributions of horizontal and amacrine cells, additions to the model could capture the contribution of these interneuron types and elucidate their computational role.
source: Insofar as surrounds reflect the contributions of horizontal and amacrine cells (Mangel, 1991; Cook and McReynolds, 1998; McMahon et al., 2004; Ichinose and Lukasiewicz, 2005; Davenport et al., 2008), additions to the model could capture the contribution of these interneuron types and elucidate their computational role.
evidence: This is speculation about potential model extensions, supported by citations.

claim: Incorporating inhibitory interneurons could also improve the accuracy of subunit estimation, if other components in the current model are indirectly absorbing their effects.
source: Incorporating inhibitory interneurons could also improve the accuracy of subunit estimation, if other components in the current model are indirectly absorbing their effects.
evidence: This is speculation about potential improvements to the model.

claim: The logic of the linearity test and the structure of the model assume linearity of the cone signal, which is a reasonable approximation for weak stimuli.
source: Specifically, the logic of the linearity test (Figure 1), and the structure of the model (Figure 2), assume linearity of the cone signal, which is a reasonable approximation for weak stimuli (Schnapf et al., 1990), but fails for stronger stimuli (J Angueyra and F Rieke, personal communication).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a model assumption and its limitations, supported by citation and personal communication.

claim: Cone nonlinearity may account for the moderately lower predictive accuracy of the model when fit to noise and tested on stronger increment-decrement stimuli.
source: This may account for the moderately lower predictive accuracy of the model when fit to noise and tested on stronger increment-decrement stimuli (Figure 7).
evidence: This is speculation about the source of reduced model accuracy in certain conditions.

claim: The model would be enhanced by allowing for temporal nonlinearities (rather than static ones), post-spike temporal filtering, more complex spike generation, and perhaps nonlinearities that vary across subunits.
source: The model would also be enhanced by allowing for temporal nonlinearities (rather than static ones) (Borghuis et al., 2013), post-spike temporal filtering (Pillow et al., 2008), more complex spike generation, and perhaps nonlinearities that vary across subunits.
evidence: This is a discussion of potential model enhancements, with some supported by citations.

claim: The model should be extended to include mechanisms for luminance and contrast gain control, both of which are essential for natural vision.
source: More generally, the model should be extended to include mechanisms for luminance and contrast gain control (Mante et al., 2008), both of which are essential for natural vision.
evidence: This is a discussion of important model extensions, supported by citation.

claim: Subunit models have been used to explain pooling behaviors in primary and secondary visual cortex.
source: Subunit models have been used to explain pooling behaviors in primary and secondary visual cortex (Hubel and Wiesel, 1959; Rust et al., 2005; Vintch et al., 2012; Freeman et al., 2013; Lochmann et al., 2013), and may represent a 'canonical' computation of sensory processing (Fukushima, 1980; Douglas et al., 1989; Heeger et al., 1996; Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999).
evidence: This is a summary of previous literature on subunit models in cortex.

claim: Subunit models may represent a 'canonical' computation of sensory processing.
source: Subunit models have been used to explain pooling behaviors in primary and secondary visual cortex (Hubel and Wiesel, 1959; Rust et al., 2005; Vintch et al., 2012; Freeman et al., 2013; Lochmann et al., 2013), and may represent a 'canonical' computation of sensory processing (Fukushima, 1980; Douglas et al., 1989; Heeger et al., 1996; Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999).
evidence: This is speculation about the generality of subunit computations, supported by citations.

claim: Eyes were enucleated from 15 terminally anesthetized macaque monkeys (M. mulatta and M. fascicularis).
source: Eyes were enucleated from 15 terminally anesthetized macaque monkeys (M. mulatta and M. fascicularis) used by other experimenters in accordance with institutional guidelines for the care and use of animals.

claim: No systematic differences in retinal physiology were observed between categories of animals.
source: No systematic differences in retinal physiology were observed between categories of animals.

claim: Segments of peripheral retina (eccentricity 5.5–13.8 mm temporal equivalent) were used for recordings.
source: Segments of peripheral retina (eccentricity 5.5–13.8 mm temporal equivalent [Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002]) that were well attached to the pigment epithelium were dissected and placed flat, RGC side down, on a planar array of extracellular microelectrodes.
evidence: This describes the retinal regions used in the experiments.

claim: The array consisted of 512 electrodes in an isosceles triangular lattice with 30 μm spacing, covering a hexagonal region 450 μm on a side.
source: The array consisted of 512 electrodes in an isosceles triangular lattice with 30 μm spacing, covering a hexagonal region 450 μm on a side (Field et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the recording array.

claim: At the mean background illumination level of the OLED display, the photoisomerization rates for the rods, L, M, and S cones were approximately 29,120, 9440, 9270, and 2320 photoisomerizations per receptor per second.
source: At the mean background illumination level of the OLED display, the photoisomerization rates for the rods, L, M, and S cones were approximately 29,120, 9440, 9270, and 2320 photoisomerizations per receptor per second (4670, 2200, 2200, 900 for the CRT display).
